notes: \cpara{Sets up the imaginary factory: blue eggs, called ``bleggs,'' and red cubes, called ``rubes,'' go into two bins.}
\cpara{Adds the correlated features: bleggs are also furred, flexible and opaque; rubes smooth, hard and translucent.}
\cpara{Introduces the first odd case, a purple egg.}
\cpara{States the objection from definitions: a blegg was defined as blue, so a purple object is not one.}
\cpara{Answers it from the other features: the object is furred, flexible and opaque, so it seems ``a strangely colored blegg.''}
\cpara{Calls in Susan the Senior Sorter.}

\cpara{The dialogue. Asked why the two bins exist, Susan gives no reason beyond the definitions (``otherwise they'd be all mixed up'') until she mentions that bleggs contain vanadium and rubes palladium. The joke carries the point: the category matters because of something it predicts.}
\cpara{Proposes a new essence, vanadium, and says the surface features matter only as clues to it.}
\cpara{States that definition, ``vanadium-containing object,'' in order to knock it down.}
\cpara{Knocks it down with made-up figures: about 98 per cent of ordinary bleggs contain vanadium, fewer of the unusual ones.}
\cpara{Gives the decisive case: an ordinary-looking blegg that contains palladium.}
\cpara{Shows the two uses of the category pulling apart: the object goes in the rube bin, but it should be expected to glow like a blegg.}
\cpara{Asks whether it is ``really'' a blegg.}
\cpara{Answers with both uses: for sorting it counts as a rube; for inferring unknown properties it belongs with the bleggs.}
\cpara{States the thesis: the same category question stands for different practical questions on different occasions.}
\cpara{Adds the corollary: a category question that stands for no practical question does not matter.}

\cfact{The same test is what William James called the pragmatic method.'' In \textsc{Pragmatism} (1907) a camping party argues whether a man circling a tree goes round the squirrel on it. James answers that it ``depends on what you practically mean by `going round' the squirrel,'' and gives the rule: ``If no practical difference whatever can be traced, then the alternatives mean practically the same thing, and all dispute is idle.'' For the earlier statement by Peirce, see the notes on ``Making Beliefs Pay Rent.''}

\cpara{Applies the idea to two disputes: whether atheism is a ``religion'' and whether transhumanism is a ``cult.'' The account of what the other side is ``really'' arguing is offered with ``(I think)'' and quotes no one; the exchange it draws on is the hypothetical one in the linked post, ``Uncritical Supercriticality.''}

\cpara{Locates the error: using a dictionary to settle whether two empirical clusters differ. The claim is limited to that use. The author returns to dictionaries in ``Disputing Definitions'' and ``The Argument from Common Usage.''}
\cpara{Says that people often do not see that a dispute about a boundary is a dispute about which characteristics to infer.}
\cpara{Names the idea.}
